title: The Science of Friendship
description: Why are friendships so central to our daily lives? This class explores the causes and consequences of this fundamental human bond, traversing its roots in animal behavior, its underlying biology and psychology, its relationship with health, and both its diversity and universal features across human cultures.

title: European Prehistory
description: Explores the archaeological record of human societies in Europe from the Upper Paleolithic to the Iron Age, a 40,000-year period. Lectures focus on specific sites and questions about culture change. We explore the evidence for subsistence and production, funerary rites, changes in settlement, production of art, symbolism, the role of technology, and emergence of social hierarchies.

title: Independent Readings in Anthropology
description: Intended for students who know their own reading needs. Normally requires regular meeting with the instructor.
prerequisites_raw: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Anthropology.

title: Independent Studies in Anthropology
description: Students must execute a limited research project on their own initiative.
prerequisites_raw: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Anthropology.

title: Undergraduate Research Assistance Training in Anthropology
description: Student gains research experience through assisting faculty member in research project.

title: Classical Archaeological Theory
description: A survey and critique of archaeological theory from the nineteenth century through the 1970's, with emphasis on shifting paradigms and the implications for research.

title: Contemporary Archaeology Theory
description: A survey and critique or archaeological theory from the 1980's to the present, emphasizing the diversity of new approaches and their implications for research.

title: Advanced Topics in Primatology
description: Exploratory discussion of major topics in primate behavioral ecology, cognition and evolution.
prerequisites_raw: None, this is a graduate course.

title: Race, Racism, and Anti-racism in Anthropology
description: A critical review of Anthropology's engagements with race, racism, and anti-racism, past and present.

title: Ethics and the Profession of Anthropology
description: A critical review of political and legal issues involved in the practice of anthropology, past and present.

title: Current Problems in Archaeology
description: Critical examination of a selected aspect of contemporary archaeological research and theory. Topics will vary from year to year.

description: A problem-oriented seminar focusing on major issues in the archaeology of hunter-gatherers.

title: Anthropological Political Economy
description: A Marxist perspective on topics such as: state formation, infrastructure, accumulation, neoliberalism, culture and class, land and labor, structure and process.

title: Applying Evolutionary Anthropology
description: Exploratory discussion of the potential of evolutionary anthropology to critique and inform the actions of the international development sector.

title: Basic Issues in Physical Anthropology
description: A review of basic issues in physical anthropology for graduate students in archaeology.

title: Religion and Ethnography: Theory, Praxis, Experience
description: An introduction to the social scientific study of religion through the lens of the ethnographic method. Attends both to practical questions concerning the performance of qualitative research and to ethnography as a literary genre that captures the complexities of lived experience. Reading assignments may be divided into three categories: historical investigations of ethnographic theory and fieldwork praxis; close examinations of discrete religious sites; and interdisciplinary meditations on such themes as interpretation, ethics, authority, and cultural translation.

title: The Archaeology of Gender
description: Reviews gendered approaches to the past. We consider the development of this area of inquiry from the initial critiques concerning the invisibility of women in the past, to a consideration of gender as a relationship between men, women, children.
